title: Intensive Sleep Retraining and Total Sleep Deprivation for Treating Chronic Insomnia: A Randomised Controlled Trial

sections.abstract: The aim of the study was to compare the efficacy of intensive sleep retraining (ISR) and total sleep deprivation (TSD) against a no‐treatment control condition for treating chronic insomnia and examine two potential mechanisms: the resolution of conditioned insomnia and the increase in homeostatic sleep drive produced by sleep deprivation. Thirty‐four adults with chronic sleep onset insomnia (with or without sleep maintenance difficulties) were randomised to ISR, TSD, or a control condition. The ISR condition consisted of a 38.5‐h period of sleep deprivation, the last 21 h of which included 42 sleep onset trials; the TSD condition consisted of an equivalent 38.5‐h sleep deprivation period without any sleep onset trials, and the control condition consisted of one night of habitual sleep in the laboratory. Significant decreases in insomnia severity were observed from pre‐ to post‐treatment in both ISR and TSD, but not in the control condition. A significant reduction in sleep onset latency was observed during the same period for the ISR condition, but not for the TSD or control conditions, with no clinically meaningful change in anxiety or depressive symptoms. Significant decreases in fatigue were also observed for both ISR and TSD conditions during the same period. These results were generally significant at 3 months after treatment. Sleep improvements produced by ISR, and to a lesser extent by TSD, suggest that both the resolution of conditioned insomnia and the increase in homeostatic sleep drive represent important mechanisms responsible for the efficacy of ISR.
sections.introduction:
Approximately 20% to 25% of adults report occasional insomnia symptoms, and 10% to 16% meet the criteria for an insomnia disorder (Morin and Jarrin 2022 ; Morin et al. 2024 ). Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT‐I) is the recommended first‐line treatment by researchers (Edinger et al. 2021 ; Qaseem et al. 2016 ; Riemann et al. 2017 ) and all professional clinical and medical associations (e.g., ESRS, SRS, CSS, ASA). CBT‐I is considered to be the most effective non‐pharmacological treatment for chronic insomnia with or without comorbidity (Kay‐Stacey and Attarian 2016 ), with clinical benefits lasting longer than medication (Jacobs et al. 2004 ; Morin et al. 1999 , 2009 ; Sivertsen et al. 2006 ; Wu et al. 2006 ). Sleep restriction intervention and stimulus control therapy are the most efficacious components of CBT‐I (Harvey et al. 2014 ).

CBT‐I is typically delivered in six sessions over a period of six to eight weeks (Bollu and Kaur 2019 ). A delayed therapeutic response (3–4 weeks), some residual daytime sleepiness early in treatment, and compliance difficulties represent common challenges associated with CBT‐I (Bootzin and Epstein 2000 ). Approximately 20% to 30% of patients are refractory to this therapy for insomnia (Morin et al. 1999 , 2009 ). The lack of response can often be explained by patients compliance issues such as: not completing sleep diaries, not adhering to the prescribed bedtime and wake‐up times, not getting out of bed during the night when unable to sleep, not staying out of bed long enough during the night for sufficient sleepiness to build up, and daytime napping (Walker et al. 2022 ). Therefore, efforts to explore other therapeutic options for chronic insomnia are warranted.

Intensive sleep retraining (ISR) is a promising treatment alternative for individuals who do not respond or respond only partially to CBT‐I. ISR involves multiple and repeated opportunities to fall asleep quickly (i.e., 20–25 min opportunity every 30 min) scheduled over a period of up to 24 h in the laboratory. Participants are awakened shortly after falling asleep, as determined by polysomnography (PSG), to preserve a homeostatic sleep drive (Lack et al. 2017 ). To facilitate sleep onset, a sleep restriction night is usually recommended on the night prior to treatment. Two preliminary studies have shown that ISR produces rapid therapeutic benefits, typically within the first week of completing treatment, with results generally maintained for up to 6 months (Harris et al. 2012 , 2007 ). In a recent uncontrolled pilot study using smartphone‐delivered ISR at home, ISR seemed to achieve similar outcomes (Mair et al. 2022 ). Overall, those studies found significant reductions in diary‐measured sleep onset latency (SOL) and increases in total sleep time (TST) and sleep efficiency (SE) (Scott et al. 2023 ). ISR is hypothesised to operate through therapeutic mechanisms similar to those involved with sleep restriction and stimulus control interventions, but with the distinct advantage of producing faster benefits owing to its implementation over a shorter period (Lack et al. 2017 ).

Three potential mechanisms of action (acting alone or in combination) are presumed to be responsible for the efficacy of ISR: (1) the resolution of conditioned insomnia, (2) the increase in homeostatic sleep drive following the near‐total sleep deprivation, and (3) the feedback about the experience of falling asleep. The resolution of conditioned insomnia is thought to be the most important mechanism accounting for long‐term sleep improvements in the ISR treatment (Scott et al. 2023 ), resulting from a gradual strengthening of the bed and bedroom as cues for sleep, as with stimulus control therapy (Bootzin and Epstein 2011 ). The rapid sleep onset is conceptualised as a reinforced learning trial, which counters the conditioned psychophysiological arousal (Spielman and Glovinsky 2012 ). However, because sleep deprivation is an implicit component of ISR, it is difficult to delineate whether its primary mechanism of action is solely through the resolution of conditioned insomnia or via the increase in the sleep drive produced by sleep deprivation. Also, since the sleep pressure from the near‐total sleep deprivation likely dissipates in the days following treatment, it may not fully explain the long‐term efficacy of ISR (Scott et al. 2023 ). To our knowledge, there has been no investigation specifically examining how ISR works.

The present study was designed to evaluate the efficacy of ISR for treating insomnia and explore its potential mechanisms of action. Specifically, it sought to determine whether the resolution of conditioned insomnia is the main therapeutic ingredient of ISR or whether the increase in homeostatic sleep drive due to sleep deprivation accounts for sleep improvements. To isolate those two components, this study compared the short‐and long‐term efficacy of ISR and total sleep deprivation (TSD) for the treatment of chronic insomnia in comparison to a control condition.
sections.methods:
Participants were recruited through social media advertisements, email lists of university community members, and advertisements on the sleep lab website between November 2020 and April 2022. Of the 275 individuals who completed the telephone screening, 103 completed a 2‐week online sleep diary. From these, 50 were deemed eligible to participate and completed a face‐to‐face clinical sleep/insomnia and psychological evaluation. Of those, 37 underwent a screening overnight PSG at home. Figure 1 illustrates participant flow through each stage of the study.

Flow diagram of participants through each stage of the study.

Inclusion criteria were: (a) age between 18 and 60 years old; (b) diagnosis of chronic insomnia based on DSM‐5 criteria; (c) SOL ≥ 30 min for ≥ 3 nights per week for 2 weeks as measured by a daily sleep diary; (d) SE ≤ 85% for 2 weeks as measured by a sleep diary; (e) significant distress or impairment of daytime functioning (score of at least 2 on item 5 or 7 of the insomnia severity index [ISI]); (f) have access to a computer with an Internet connection to complete questionnaires.

Exclusion criteria were: (a) active or unstable progressive medical condition (e.g., cancer) or degenerative neurological disease (e.g., dementia); (b) current diagnosis of major depression, dysthymia, or anxiety disorders; (c) lifetime diagnosis of any psychotic or bipolar disorder; (d) other sleep disorders, sleep apnea (apnea/hypopnea index > 15), restless legs, or periodic limb movements during sleep (movement index with arousal > 15/h); (e) alcohol or substance use disorder in the past 12 months; (f) use of any drug known to affect sleep (e.g., cocaine) in the past 2 weeks; (g) current or planned pregnancy during the study; (h) night shift work or irregular sleep pattern (e.g., usual bedtime after 2:00 a.m. or usual wake time after 10:00 a.m.); (i) current suicidal risk; (j) body mass index > 32; (k) use of sleep‐inducing drugs (prescription or non‐prescription); (l) use of tobacco products.

Patients with stable medical (e.g., hypertension) or psychiatric (e.g., anxiety) conditions were included in the study if these conditions were not the primary cause of the insomnia and that no medication known to alter sleep was taken for the condition. For depression, it had to be in remission (with or without treatment) and the participant had to have no more than two lifetime episodes of major depression. Participants using prescribed or over‐the‐counter sleep medications, cannabis, or alcohol to promote sleep were required to discontinue such practises at least 2 weeks prior to the screening stage. Participants were also instructed to avoid alcohol 24 h before laboratory assessment and to consume no more than three coffee or caffeinated beverages per day for the duration of the study.

Financial compensation of up to $330 CAD, depending on the study requirements completed, and a summary of PSG test results were provided to the participants upon completion of the study. Ethical approval was obtained from the Research Ethics Committee in Neurosciences and Mental Health of the Centre intégré universitaire de santé et de services sociaux de la Capitale‐Nationale (CIUSSS‐CN, approval #2021–2015) and all participants signed written informed consent. Study data were collected and managed using REDCap electronic data capture tools hosted at University Laval (Harris et al. 2019 , 2009 ).

The Diagnostic Interview for Insomnia is an abbreviated version of the Insomnia Interview Schedule (Morin 1993 ) used to assess the nature and severity of insomnia, sleep history, use of sleep medication or other drugs that may affect sleep, medical history, and screening for other sleep disorders.

The International Neuropsychiatric Mini‐Interview version 7.0.2 (Sheehan et al. 1998 ) is a structured diagnostic interview used to document current and past psychiatric problems and exclude participants with comorbid psychiatric disorders (e.g., major depressive disorder, generalised anxiety disorder).

Figure 2 illustrates the study protocol timeline. All questionnaires were administered at the end of each evaluation period.

Study protocol timeline.

The ISI (Bastien et al. 2001 ; Morin 1993 ) is a seven‐item patient‐reported measure that assesses perceived severity of sleep difficulties, daytime impairments, and distress about sleep disturbances in the past month. A higher score (0–28) indicates more severe insomnia, within four severity categories: absence of insomnia (0–7); sub‐threshold insomnia (8–14); moderate insomnia (15–21); severe insomnia (22–28). Participants with a change score greater than seven relative to baseline are considered treatment responders, and participants with an absolute score of less than 8 were considered treatment remitters. The ISI has adequate psychometric properties and is sensitive in measuring treatment response (Morin et al. 2011 ).

The sleep diary is a self‐reported measure used to gather data on the following variables: bedtime, SOL, number and duration of nighttime awakenings, wake after sleep onset (WASO), sleep quality, daytime naps, use of medication, and alcohol for sleep. Participants were instructed to complete the sleep diary daily within 1 h of getting out of bed in the morning during each assessment period. The sleep variables derived from the diary and used in the current study were SOL, WASO, TST, and SE (the percentage of total sleep time out of the amount of time spent in bed). The sleep diary is recommended for tracking treatment effects (Buysse et al. 2006 ; Carney et al. 2012 ).

The actigraphy is an ambulatory monitoring device that is placed on the wrist of participants to continuously record sleep‐awake activity during each assessment period. Data were sampled in 30‐s epochs and analysed using Actiware Software version 6 (algorithm 40) (Respironics, Bend, OR) and all recordings were visually inspected prior to analysis to check for artefacts and malfunctions. Daily self‐reported bedtimes and awakening times reported on the sleep diaries were used to cross‐validate and set the intervals for analyses of actigraphy recordings. Participants were instructed to remove the device when entering water or when exercising vigorously. The sleep variables SOL, WASO, TST, and SE were estimated by automatic scoring in the present study. The actigraphy has been validated in a study involving individuals with insomnia (Vallières and Morin 2003 ).

PSG was used for one ambulatory night during the screening phase to screen for other sleep disorders, during the sleep restriction night for adaptation, and during the ISR protocol to determine sleep onset and total sleep time. Participants in the other two conditions were required to wear the same montage as those in the ISR condition for the 21‐h protocol in the laboratory. Data were recorded using TWin software and 32‐channel Grass amplifiers (Astro‐Med Inc., West Warwick, RI). A full montage was used for the screening night to rule out other sleep disorders; it included electroencephalography (F3‐A2, F4‐A1, C3‐A2, C4‐A1, O1‐A2, O2‐A1 channels), submental electromyography, bilateral electrooculography and electrocardiogram, nasal/oral airflow, respiratory effort bands, finger pulse oximetry (SaO 2 ), and bilateral anterior tibialis electromyography. During the sleep restriction night and the 21‐h protocol, all participants had a standard PSG montage. During the ISR protocol, sleep onset was determined when alpha waves were present in less than 50% of each 30‐s epoch for three consecutive epochs (Carskadon et al. 1986 ). Certified technicians were responsible for the installation and scoring records, which were performed according to the standards of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (Iber et al. 2007 ). The following variables of the night of sleep restriction were analysed: SOL, WASO, TST, and SE.

The Flinders Fatigue Scale (FFS) is a self‐reported and validated seven‐item questionnaire that measures various characteristics of daytime fatigue experienced over the past two weeks. Higher scores (0–31) indicate greater fatigue. A description of the term “fatigue” is provided in the questionnaire instructions (Cameron et al. 2017 ).

The patient health questionnaire (PHQ‐9) is a self‐reported and validated nine‐item questionnaire that assesses nine symptoms of depression over the past 2 weeks. Total scores range from 0 to 27, with higher scores indicating more severe depressive symptoms, within five severity categories: none‐minimal (0–4); mild (5–9); moderate (10–14); moderately severe (15–19); severe (20–27) (Kroenke et al. 2001 ).

The Generalised Anxiety Disorder Scale (GAD‐7) is a self‐reported and validated seven‐item questionnaire that assesses seven symptoms of anxiety over the past 2 weeks. Total scores range from 0 to 21, with a higher score indicating more severe anxiety symptoms within four severity categories: minimal (0–4); mild (5–9); moderate (10–14); severe (15–21) (Spitzer et al. 2006 ).

Visual analogue scales were used to assess sleepiness and emotional state during the last 12 h of the treatment period. Participants were asked to circle a number from 0 to 10 corresponding to their current state on each of the following dimensions: fully awake (0) to very sleepy (10); not at all irritable (0) to very irritable (10); not at all sad (0) to very sad (10); not at all happy (0) to very happy (10); not at all angry (0) to very angry (10). Participants were asked to complete the analogue scales every hour from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., for a total of 13 times, without access to their response history.

The pre‐treatment period consisted of two consecutive weeks and was scheduled from Thursday to Thursday to coordinate the treatment period over the weekends. At the end of the pre‐treatment period, participants were informed of their assignment to one of the three conditions. Participants were required to come to the sleep laboratory on Thursday at 7:00 p.m. for the night. Their time in bed was restricted to 6.5 h (11:00 p.m. to 5:30 a.m.) to increase homeostatic sleep pressure before treatment. After waking up, participants were asked to leave the laboratory and resume their normal daytime activities, but daytime naps were not allowed. All participants were asked to come back to the laboratory at 7:00 p.m. on Friday.

The 21‐h treatment period was scheduled from 11:00 p.m. on Friday to 8:00 p.m. on Saturday. Participants in both the ISR and TSD conditions experienced at least 38.5 h of sleep deprivation, from 5:30 a.m. Friday through 8:00 p.m. Saturday. Time was set aside to re‐explain the protocol, answer questions, reassess suicide risk, and calibrate the PSG montage. Participants were continuously monitored throughout the laboratory period to ensure that they were following the instructions specific to their condition. They were provided with breakfast, lunch, dinner, and snacks, but were not allowed to consume caffeine or alcohol or to exercise. The light level in the rooms was kept consistent during the entire study period. After the ISR and TSD interventions, participants were not allowed to drive home for safety reasons and were instead picked up by a person or provided with a taxi voucher. No information about CBT‐I, sleep education, or sleep hygiene was provided to any of the participants during the study.

This procedure involved a series of 42 consecutive, half‐hour sleep onset opportunities, repeated every 30 min starting at 11:00 p.m. At the beginning of each trial, participants were instructed to lie down in bed, close their eyes, and relax. They were left alone in the bedroom, the lights were turned off, and the door was closed. The sleep opportunities began when the lights were turned off. Once sleep onset was detected by the recording technician, participants were allowed to sleep for 2 to 4 consecutive minutes before being awakened. If participants did not fall asleep, the trial ended after 25 min, with a five‐minute interval before the next sleep attempt. Participants were not given feedback about whether they fell asleep or not. Between trials, participants were instructed to get out of bed, leave the room, and either sit in a chair or stand in another room. They could talk with the experimenter or read but could not watch television or use a computer.

Participants were instructed to remain awake during the 21‐h treatment period. They could engage in quiet activities in the laboratory (e.g., reading, watching TV, using the computer) or talk with the experimenter. They could not sleep or stay in their bedrooms. A research assistant was always present to ensure that they remained awake.

Participants were allowed to sleep for up to 8 h starting at 11:00 p.m. While awake, they could engage in quiet activities in the laboratory (e.g., reading, watching television, using the computer) but were not allowed to sleep or stay in the bedroom during the day. They could attend a 1.5‐h information session about CBT‐I after completing the 1‐month follow‐up assessment.

After the laboratory period, all participants were instructed to resume their normal sleep–wake schedule. The post‐treatment period involved two consecutive weeks immediately after the treatment protocol. The first 2 days were not included in the analyses to reduce the potential confounding effects of acute sleep deprivation rebound on sleep variables (Bonnet 1985 ). Follow‐up consisted of one consecutive week beginning 3, 7, and 11 weeks after the treatment period.

G*Power software version 3.1.9.4 (Faul et al. 2007 ) was used to conduct an a priori sensitivity‐type power analysis for the SOL and WASO variables. The planned total number of participants across treatment conditions was 24 (12 per condition), with the possibility of completing five measurement times, for a maximum possible of 120 observations (96 after accounting for 20% expected attrition). Based on standard power conditions (80% power, alpha = 5% two‐tailed; Cohen 1988 ), the minimally detectable effect size was a moderate effect ( d = 0.5), that is, a reduction of 18 min in SOL (calculated as d × standard deviation; 0.5 × 35) and 32 min (0.5 × 63) in WASO, which is realistic given the reductions of 30 and 28 min observed in a previous study using ISR at post‐treatment (Harris et al. 2007 ).

A total of 36 participants were randomised to one of the three conditions, and 34 were included in the final analyses. Two participants, one from the TSD condition and one from the control condition, dropped out during the pre‐treatment period due to scheduling conflicts. Randomisation to one of the three conditions was stratified according to participant age (≤ 49 years old and ≥ 50 years old) and the insomnia severity as documented by the screening ISI score (≤ 14 and ≥ 15). Assignment to the three conditions was determined by a computer‐generated randomisation programme with a block size of 3, managed by the biostatistician (HI).

Main analyses were performed using SAS 9.4 TSM8 statistical software with a standard two‐tailed alpha of 5%. The primary dependent variable was the ISI. Secondary outcome measures of sleep, fatigue, anxiety, and depression were also included. One‐way ANOVAs and chi‐squared tests were used to compare between‐condition differences in sociodemographic and clinical characteristics.

To examine changes in outcome variables within and between conditions, 3 (conditions) × 5 (times pre‐treatment, post‐treatment, 1‐month, 2‐month and 3‐month follow‐up) split‐plot mixed model analyses were calculated to test condition, time, and interaction effects, using their baseline means as a covariate control. Linear mixed models (Brown and Prescott 2006 ) were preferred to avoid the need for imputation of missing data. Condition × time interactions (significant or not) were decomposed using simple effects to test and compare temporal changes within and between each treatment condition. Effect sizes for changes from pre‐ to post‐treatment and pre‐treatment to follow‐up 3 were calculated as the difference between means divided by the root mean squared error of the mixed model. Effect sizes were interpreted according to Cohen's criteria (Cohen 1992 ).
sections.results:
Table 1 shows the demographic and clinical characteristics of the participants in the treatment and control conditions. There were no significant differences between conditions on age, sex, marital status, occupation, years of education, length of insomnia, body mass index, SOL, WASO, TST, SE, ISI, respiratory disturbance index, and periodic limb movements in sleep with arousal index at screening. The ISR condition had significantly more participants with mixed sleep onset and maintenance insomnia (10) compared with the TSD condition (4), but treatment conditions were not significantly different from the control. None of the participants reported having received CBT‐I.

Demographic and clinical characteristics at screening.

Note : Values with different letters differ significantly ( p < 0.05).

All 34 participants completed the study protocol and complied with the 6.5‐h sleep restriction period prior to the implementation of the treatment protocol. One‐way ANOVAs indicated that there were no significant differences between conditions in SOL, WASO, TST, and SE on PSG and sleep diary ( p > 0.05) during the sleep restriction night. Among participants assigned to the ISR treatment, 96% of the 499 sleep onset trials occurred within the 25‐min window, with an average SOL of 5.31 min (SD = 2.08) and an average sleep time of 3.18 min (SD = 0.43). Due to the COVID‐19 lockdown curfew, five sleep onset trials were cancelled.

Adjusted means, change scores (∆), and Cohen's d values across time and condition for the ISI are displayed in Table 2 . No significant condition × time interactions were observed. Paired comparisons were performed between the active treatments and control condition at post‐treatment and 1 month after treatment and between active treatments at 2 and 3 months after treatment.

From pre‐ to post‐treatment, significant decreases in insomnia severity were observed in both ISR (∆ = −3.91 points, p < 0.001, d = −1.32) and TSD (∆ = −3.66 points, p < 0.001, d = −1.23). ISI reductions observed in the ISR and TSD conditions combined (∆ = −3.79 points) were significantly greater ( p < 0.001, one‐tailed) compared to the control condition (∆ = 0) at post‐treatment. From pre‐treatment to 3‐month follow‐up, significant decreases in insomnia severity were observed in both ISR (∆ = −5.91 points, p < 0.001, d = −1.99) and TSD (∆ = −5.41 points, p < 0.001, d = −1.82). Mean pre‐treatment ISI scores (16.3) were in the moderate severity range and fell into the subthreshold insomnia category at post‐treatment for both ISR (12.4) and TSD (12.6) conditions and remained in that range at follow‐ups. No significant differences were found between ISR and TSD for any follow‐up.

Percentage of treatment responders and remitters based on ISI scores are displayed in Table 2 . The proportions of responders (16.67% for ISR and 8.33% TSD) and remitters (8.33% for ISR and 16.67% for TSD) were equivalent at post‐treatment and between active treatments at 1, 2, and 3 months after treatment.

sections.discussion:
The aim of this study was to compare the efficacy of ISR and TSD for treating chronic insomnia and to examine two mechanisms of action. ISR and TSD were compared to a control condition consisting of one night of habitual sleep in the laboratory. Both treatments reduced the severity of insomnia and fatigue symptoms compared to the control condition. Sleep improvements were also observed in both treatment conditions as demonstrated by a decrease in WASO and an increase in SE at post‐treatment on the sleep diary. ISR produced larger effect sizes for SOL and TST relative to TSD at post‐treatment. Overall, improvements were significant at 3 months after treatment. Although the resolution of conditioned insomnia is thought to be the most important mechanism of action accounting for sleep improvements produced by the ISR treatment (Scott et al. 2023 ), the present findings suggest that the experience of total sleep deprivation may be a major contributor to ISR‐produced sleep improvements.

The novelty of this study was the addition of a sleep deprivation intervention, which allowed isolating more clearly the two potential mechanisms of action associated with ISR. Because SOL was improved with both ISR and TSD, one can argue that ISR works, not only because of its reconditioning process, but also because of its inherent sleep deprivation component which strengthens the homeostatic sleep drive. In addition, WASO improved similarly for both treatments on the sleep diary measure. This finding suggests that the strengthening of the homeostatic sleep drive may play a role in improving sleep‐maintenance insomnia.

The repeated sleep onset trials involved with ISR may target the pre‐sleep behaviours occurring around the initial sleep onset period, but this benefit may not necessarily generalise to subsequent awakenings during the night. In this regard, the reconditioning process seems to affect mostly the first sleep onset episode, which is normally characterised by the following sequence of behaviours: walking to the bedroom, getting into the bed, turning off the light, closing the eyes, and falling asleep. Therefore, the newly learned response of falling asleep rapidly at bedtime may not entirely generalise to later awakenings during the night due to different insomnia cues. This would be consistent with the relatively greater effect sizes in the ISR condition for the decrease of SOL rather than the decrease of WASO.

While sleep deprivation used as an intervention has been studied primarily for its antidepressant effect, it may also play an important role in improving sleep in chronic insomnia. Sleep deprivation has been shown to produce rapid antidepressant effects for about 40% to 60% of all depressed patients (Boland et al. 2017 ), with improvements occurring within hours (Hemmeter et al. 2010 ). Despite such rapid relief of depressive symptoms, sleep deprivation has not been widely accepted for treating depression because of the rapid reversal of symptoms upon sleep recovery (Wirz‐Justice and Van den Hoofdakker 1999 ). However, the fact that the reduced depression symptoms extended through the 3‐month follow‐up period suggests that the insomnia‐associated depression is probably due to more than the simple acute sleep deprivation that is reversed with recovery sleep. It may address some of the fears shown by insomnia patients regarding the loss of sleep. The fact that the sleep loss was not an aversive experience (as evidenced by the visual analogue scales) could address some of the beliefs generally held by insomnia patients that are thought to exacerbate the insomnia and symptoms of depression.

CBT‐I, which includes a sleep restriction component, has been shown to be effective in treating people with insomnia and comorbid depression (Manber et al. 2008 ; Sweetman et al. 2020 ; Taylor et al. 2007 ). Similarly, the sleep improvements observed with ISR treatment might be partly explained by the increased homeostatic sleep drive induced by sleep deprivation. Both TSD and sleep restriction increase homeostatic sleep drive (Goel et al. 2013 ) and are likely to improve sleep on subsequent nights.

Very few studies have examined the recovery sleep period following TSD in adults with insomnia. In subjects with or without insomnia, aged 55 to 71 years, after 64 h of TSD, SE returned to baseline by the second recovery night in subjects without insomnia, but it remained elevated and improved through the fourth recovery night in subjects with insomnia (Bonnet 1986 ). Subjective sleepiness did not return to baseline levels until early in the second recovery night (Bonnet 1985 ). Another study showed that adults with primary insomnia had significantly more TST, as defined by PSG, on the first night of recovery than at baseline after one night of sleep deprivation; however, there was no additional follow‐up night to measure the time it took to return to baseline (Stepanski et al. 2000 ). The apparent extended recovery sleep after TSD in those with insomnia suggests that TSD may have a therapeutic effect.

The sleep diary results for ISR are similar to those reported in previous studies in terms of reductions in SOL and increases in TST and SE. However, the WASO reductions at post‐treatment have not been consistent across studies (Scott et al. 2023 ). Overall, findings from the current and other studies have shown that ISR produces moderate to large effect sizes for SOL (ranging from 0.61 to 1.14) and SE (0.65 to 1.12), small to moderate effect sizes for WASO (0.26 to 0.61) and moderate effect sizes for TST (0.53 to 0.77) (Harris et al. 2012 ; Mair et al. 2022 ). Additionally, the mean gain in diary‐measured TST for ISR ranged from 27.1 to 64.6 min (Harris et al. 2012 , 2007 ; Mair et al. 2022 ), which exceeded the change observed with standard CBT‐I of less than 30 min and within‐subject effect sizes of less than 0.5 (Mitchell et al. 2012 ; Morin et al. 2009 ).

Actigraphy data did not show meaningful changes in any sleep variables, which is consistent with the only previous in‐laboratory study (Harris et al. 2012 ). In comparison, sleep restriction therapy in older adults produced a decrease in SOL, WASO, and an increase in SE compared to a waitlist control, with no further changes at 3‐month and 1‐year follow‐ups, as measured by actigraphy (Epstein et al. 2012 ). A meta‐analysis and systematic review published in 2019 reported that CBT‐I produced a small effect reduction in SOL ( g = −0.28) and a moderate effect for reduction in TST ( g = −0.51) as measured by actigraphy (Mitchell et al. 2019 ). The comparison of ISR, SRT, or CBT‐I actigraphy data presents significant challenges due to the limited data available on ISR.

Treatment response and remission rates were similar for ISR and TSD and relatively low (between 8% and 33%) both at post‐treatment and follow‐ups. Using different criteria based on SOL and/or SE, Harris et al. ( 2012 ) reported higher rates (47% and 37%, respectively). In the pilot study using smartphone‐delivered ISR, the proportion of post‐treatment responders was 50% according to the ISI score (Mair et al. 2022 ). However, participants in the ISR condition had more severe insomnia symptoms at pre‐treatment (mean ISI score: 21.08) than in the current study (mean ISI score: 16.31), leaving more room for improvement. These responses are far from the 70% to 80% response rates to conventionally administered CBT‐I over 6–8 weeks (Morin et al. 2009 ).

The low treatment response and remission rates in the current study may be due in part to the absence of feedback provided to participants about whether they fell asleep or not during ISR. That feedback mechanism could enhance the therapeutic benefits of ISR (Scott et al. 2023 ). Given their average pre‐treatment sleep diary SOL of 44 min, feedback that they fell asleep on 96% of occasions within an average of 5 min could have had an impressive reassuring effect. It is well known that some people with insomnia consistently underestimate the amount of time they sleep and overestimate the amount of time they are awake (Stephan and Siclari 2023 ). One study found that providing feedback and guidance about sensor‐based sleep parameters reduced insomnia severity and sleep disturbance, although the magnitude of these benefits was modest (Spina et al. 2023 ). More research is needed to evaluate the potential added benefits of providing feedback to participants about their sleep onset trials. Finally, a home‐based ISR should theoretically result in better sleep improvements because the treatment takes place where the conditioned insomnia typically occurs. According to Bootzin ( 1972 ), a person with sleep problems may gradually come to associate the sleep environment with difficulty falling asleep. After repeated negative experiences, it becomes strongly associated with negative emotion. However, a study using a smartphone‐delivered ISR at home reported similar results to the laboratory‐based ISR procedure (Mair et al. 2022 ). It is difficult to assess the potential benefit of a self‐administered home‐based ISR when compared to an impressive laboratory treatment protocol. Further research should try to evaluate the potential home‐based treatment benefits, as would be suggested by Bootzin ( 1972 ).

None of the participants in the current study chose to leave during the 21‐h treatment period, although they were free to do so, a finding also reported in the two previous laboratory‐based ISR studies (Harris et al. 2012 , 2007 ). ISR appears to be well accepted by the participants. Both treatments involving 38.5 h of sleep deprivation showed no increase in negative emotions or decrease in joy in the last 12 h of the deprivation compared to the normally sleeping control condition. However, ISR should be contraindicated for individuals with untreated hypersomnolence, histories of bipolar disorder, or seizures because sleep deprivation can trigger symptoms of those conditions (Pigeon 2010 ). Safety precautions should be taken during and after the treatment, including refraining from driving. A qualitative study would be useful to gain a better understanding of the participants' experience (e.g., their experience of a robust recovery sleep following the deprivation).

Although ISR is not a first‐line treatment, it could be an alternative treatment option for patients who do not respond to standard CBT‐I, sleep restriction alone (Tse et al. 2024 ) or other treatment modalities such as third‐wave psychotherapies. For the most refractory cases and those with major comorbid psychiatric disorders, one could even envision implementing this treatment on an inpatient basis.

One key limitation is the small sample size ( N = 34) that limits the generalisability of the results as it may not fully represent clinical patients with chronic insomnia and may be insufficient to detect statistically significant differences for small effect sizes. Also, the no‐treatment control condition did not adequately control for expectations, as participants knew they were not receiving a treatment for insomnia. Finally, although the 3‐month follow‐up period provided some important insights, it is still relatively short‐term given that most participants had suffered from insomnia for an average of almost 10 years.

Strengths of this study include its randomised controlled design and the stringent eligibility criteria. These elements strengthen the internal validity of the study by minimising selection bias and providing confidence that the observed effects were due to the treatment. Additionally, the multi‐method measurements, including diary, actigraphy, and questionnaires, allowed for a comprehensive assessment of outcomes and a better understanding of ISR's efficacy and mechanisms of action. PSG measures should be considered in future research to provide valuable objective data. To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate the mechanisms of ISR, offering new insights for guiding future research.

sections.conclusion: The results of the current study suggest that ISR and, to a lesser extent, TSD produce important reductions in insomnia symptoms and sleep improvements, though the results are mixed considering the low response rates for both treatments. The findings indicate that both the resolution of the conditioned insomnia and the increase in homeostatic sleep drive are important mechanisms of change associated with ISR treatment. The resolution of the conditioned insomnia had a significant effect on reducing SOL but a more modest effect on WASO. The additional benefits of providing feedback about sleep states should be evaluated. ISR appears to be a promising treatment for sleep onset insomnia and represents a potential alternative for patients who do not respond or respond only partially to CBT‐I. In its current form, ISR treatment in the laboratory is likely to be expensive, and the potential of digital applications in the home environment should be further studied. Although ISR shows promise for treating chronic insomnia, it remains experimental. Larger randomised controlled trials are needed to determine its efficacy, effectiveness, and clinical utility for chronic insomnia.
